title: The Border Walls: Keeping the GLM Together and Apart
body:
# The Border Walls: Keeping the GLM Together and Apart

## The Perimeter

The Great Lakes Metropolitan area is not an open city. It is a fortress. The border system — referred to officially as the Perimeter Containment Infrastructure and colloquially as "the Walls" — encircles the entire GLM along a boundary roughly corresponding to the outer edges of the six-state footprint. The system is not a single wall but a layered defense-in-depth architecture combining physical barriers, sensor networks, autonomous weapons platforms, drone patrols, and digital surveillance. Its purpose is dual: keep the wastelands out and keep the labor force in.

The Walls were built in stages between 2158 and 2179, as climate migration from the coasts, the Southwest, and the Southern states overwhelmed the region's capacity to absorb newcomers. What began as temporary checkpoints on interstate highways evolved into permanent fortifications. By 2175, the GLM's corponation council had formalized the border into a unified system, funded by a shared security levy and operated by Aegis Defense Solutions, a corponation whose sole product is the Perimeter.

## Physical Barriers

The physical wall varies by terrain. Along the southern boundary — running roughly from Springfield, Illinois through Indianapolis to Columbus, Ohio — the wall is a 12-meter reinforced concrete barrier topped with sensor arrays and razor mesh. This section faces the most pressure, as climate refugees from the former Gulf states and the desiccated Mississippi Valley push north in waves. The wall here shows its age: patched sections, scorch marks from breaching attempts, and the occasional gap where subsidence has undermined the foundation.

Along the western boundary through Iowa and Minnesota, the wall is less imposing physically but more technologically dense. The terrain is flat and open, making physical barriers less effective but sensor coverage more efficient. Here, the primary defense is a network of autonomous ground stations every 500 meters, each equipped with thermal imaging, seismic sensors, and non-lethal deterrent systems — though reports of lethal force are persistent and credible. The northern boundary merges with Canadian border infrastructure, a joint operation governed by the Great Lakes Mutual Defense Compact signed in 2172.

The eastern boundary along the Appalachian foothills is the most porous. The terrain is rugged, the wall is incomplete in several stretches, and the corponations that nominally control eastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania have less incentive to invest in border security. Smuggling operations — both human and material — flow through these gaps with regularity.

## Digital Barriers

The physical wall is the visible layer. The digital barrier is arguably more effective. Every individual within the GLM carries a biometric identity profile linked to their tier status, employment records, medical history, and movement patterns. Entry into the GLM requires registration in this system; existing within the GLM without registration makes a person functionally invisible — unable to access housing, employment, medical care, or even basic nutrition dispensaries.

The digital barrier extends beyond identity management. The GLM's communications infrastructure is monitored at every level. External signals — radio, satellite, mesh network — are jammed or intercepted along the Perimeter. Internal communications are routed through corponation-controlled networks that log metadata and, in many cases, content. The border is not just a line on a map. It is a state of surveillance that begins at the wall and extends inward to every device, every transaction, every movement.

## Who Gets In

Entry into the GLM is governed by a quota system administered by the corponation council. Each year, a limited number of immigration slots are allocated based on labor demand projections. Applicants must demonstrate skills matching current workforce needs — engineering, medical, agricultural, technical maintenance — and must have a corponation sponsor willing to assume economic responsibility for the new entrant. The sponsoring corponation assigns the immigrant's tier status, which is almost always Tier 4 or 5.

In practice, the quota system is a fiction layered over a black market. Immigration brokers — some corponation-affiliated, some independent — sell entry for prices that fluctuate with demand. A healthy, skilled individual might pay the equivalent of five years' wasteland earnings for a legitimate entry visa. An unskilled individual pays more for a forged identity that may or may not survive the first biometric checkpoint. Thousands attempt illegal entry each month. Most are turned back. Some are detained in processing camps along the southern wall where conditions are deliberately harsh enough to discourage repeat attempts. Some simply disappear.

## Who Gets Out

Leaving the GLM is technically unrestricted — no corponation profits from preventing a Tier 5 laborer from walking into the wasteland. In practice, departure is complicated by the same digital infrastructure that controls entry. Leaving forfeits one's biometric profile and tier status. Re-entry is not guaranteed and rarely granted. For most residents, leaving the GLM means permanent exile into a world with no infrastructure, no medical care, and no protection.

Despite this, people leave. Some are expelled — corponations strip tier status from dissidents, criminals, and individuals deemed economically non-productive, effectively exiling them. Others leave voluntarily, driven by the calculation that a free life in the wasteland, however short, is preferable to a managed existence in Tier 5. Underground networks facilitate these departures, providing safe passage through the wall and connections to wasteland communities. These networks operate at enormous risk, as Aegis Defense Solutions classifies unauthorized wall crossings — in either direction — as security violations punishable by indefinite detention.

## The Wall as Symbol

The Perimeter Containment Infrastructure is the GLM's most honest structure. It does not pretend to be anything other than what it is: a mechanism for controlling the movement of human beings based on their assessed economic value. The corponations maintain it not out of ideology but out of calculation — an uncontrolled influx would strain resources, destabilize the tier system, and threaten the labor economics that underpin corporate profitability. The wall is expensive, imperfect, and morally indefensible. It is also, by the logic of the system that built it, entirely necessary. The GLM exists because the wall exists. That is the bargain, and every resident — from Tier 1 to Tier 5 — lives within its terms.
